notes: Ruling slot 0 = Nationalist Liberal Party (Somoza Debayle). Coalition slot 13 holds the Somoza family business-and-patronage empire as a dynastic power bloc; Guardia Nacional in slot 22. MD placements kept for PSC (1), PLI (2), FSLN (5); MD's later MUR/PRT/PLIUN replaced by PSN (4), PCdeN (19) and the Zancudo collaborationist Conservatives (6). Traditionalist Conservatives (Aguero) in slot 14. House of Clarence kept in 23.

0.name: Partido Liberal Nacionalista
0.text:
The Nationalist Liberal Party is the political vehicle of the Somoza dynasty, built by Anastasio Somoza García in the 1930s and inherited by his sons. Since May 1967 it has been led by President Anastasio Somoza Debayle, who also commands the National Guard, and it dominates Congress, the courts and local government.

The PLN combines Liberal tradition with personal loyalty to the Somozas, staunch anti-communism and unconditional alignment with the United States, which counts Nicaragua among its most reliable allies. Its strength lies in state patronage, public employees, rural caciques and the votes delivered by a machine that never loses an election.

1.name: Partido Social Cristiano
1.text:
The Social Christian Party was founded in 1957 by young Catholic professionals and students disillusioned with the old Conservative Party's deals with the Somozas. It is a small but growing opposition party, influential among university students and in the Christian labour movement.

Guided by Catholic social teaching, the PSC calls for an end to the dynasty, honest elections, agrarian reform, cooperatives and workers' rights. It rejects both Somocismo and Marxist revolution and is friendly toward Western Christian Democracy. Its leverage lies in Church networks, Christian unions and the moral authority of a new generation of opponents.

2.name: Partido Liberal Independiente
2.text:
The Independent Liberal Party was founded in 1944 by Liberals who broke with Anastasio Somoza García over his plans to remain in power. Ever since, it has carried the banner of anti-Somoza liberalism, boycotting rigged elections or joining opposition coalitions such as the 1967 National Opposition Union.

The PLI stands for constitutional government, free elections, civil liberties and the separation of the Liberal tradition from the Somoza family. It is pro-Western and moderate. Its base is among urban professionals, intellectuals and Liberal families in León, and its leverage lies in its legitimacy as the true heir of Nicaraguan liberalism.

3.name: La Prensa
3.text:
La Prensa is Nicaragua's leading opposition newspaper, directed by Pedro Joaquín Chamorro Cardenal, who has been jailed and exiled repeatedly for resisting the Somozas, most recently after the massacre of January 1967. Around the paper gathers a circle of journalists, reform-minded Conservatives and young professionals.

The La Prensa milieu calls for democracy, social justice, labour rights and an end to dynastic rule, combining Christian humanism with social-democratic reform. It is pro-Western but critical of US support for Somoza. Its leverage lies in the printed word, the respect Chamorro commands and its ability to set the agenda of the opposition.

4.name: Partido Socialista Nicaragüense
4.text:
The Nicaraguan Socialist Party was founded in 1944 as the country's pro-Soviet communist party and has been banned for most of its existence. It operates semi-clandestinely, rooted in trade unions in Managua and Chinandega, and many of the founders of the Sandinista Front began their political lives in its youth.

Loyal to Moscow, the PSN favours mass organisation, union work and broad democratic alliances against the dictatorship, and it regards guerrilla warfare as premature adventurism. It denounces US imperialism. Its leverage lies in its labour cadres and its long organisational experience.

5.name: Frente Sandinista de Liberación Nacional
5.text:
The Sandinista National Liberation Front was founded in 1961 by Carlos Fonseca Amador, Tomás Borge and Silvio Mayorga, taking its name from the guerrilla hero Augusto César Sandino. After the defeat at Pancasán in 1967 and the killing of Julio Buitrago in Managua in July 1969, it is battered, and Fonseca is in prison in Costa Rica.

The FSLN seeks the armed overthrow of the Somoza dynasty and a socialist revolution inspired by Cuba, fusing Marxism with Sandino's anti-imperialist nationalism. Its leverage lies in a small, determined network of guerrillas, students and urban militants.

6.name: Los Zancudos
6.text:
The Zancudos, or mosquitoes, is the scornful nickname for Conservative politicians who accept the minority seats and offices Somoza grants the opposition, living off the regime like insects off blood. Since the pacts of the 1950s they have provided the dynasty with a respectable conservative façade.

They defend the privileges of the old Granada families, Catholic tradition and social hierarchy, and they prefer a deal with the strongman to the risks of reform or revolution. Their leverage lies in Somoza's need for a tame opposition and in the patronage that flows to them in return.

7.name: Oficina de Seguridad Nacional
7.text:
The Office of National Security is the political police and intelligence service of the Somoza regime, operating within the National Guard. It hunts Sandinista guerrillas, watches opposition politicians and union leaders, and runs informers in schools, churches and workplaces.

The OSN treats every form of dissent as subversion and relies on arrests, interrogation and torture to protect the dynasty. It answers only to the Somoza family and the Guard command. Its leverage lies in fear, secret files and its indispensable role in keeping the regime safe.

8.name: Los Amigos del Imam Musa
8.text:
The Friends of Imam Musa are a few Lebanese Shia trading families in Managua and Granada who follow the work of Imam Musa al-Sadr, who has just founded the Supreme Islamic Shia Council in Lebanon. They gather privately for religious holidays and support relatives back home.

The circle shares al-Sadr's message of education, social justice and dignity for the poor and favours peaceful integration in Nicaragua. It stays out of politics, but its commercial networks within the Arab merchant community give it modest economic weight.

9.name: Los Hijos del Ayatolá
9.text:
The Sons of the Ayatollah are a handful of young Shia of Lebanese origin who have brought back from the Middle East the sermons of Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini, exiled in Najaf, and his teaching that the Islamic jurist should govern. They meet secretly in private homes in Managua.

They denounce both superpowers and dream of a revolutionary Islamic order, and some admire the anti-imperialist zeal of the Sandinistas. They have no prospects in Catholic Nicaragua, but their radicalism and foreign contacts make them a curiosity the security police keep an eye on.

10.name: Los Peregrinos de Managua
10.text:
The Pilgrims of Managua are a small association of Sunni Muslim merchants of Palestinian origin who have made the pilgrimage to Mecca and keep in touch with the Muslim World League. They organise prayers, religious lessons and charity within a largely Christian Arab immigrant community.

They preach piety, obedience to established rulers and moral conservatism, and they share the regime's anti-communism. Their leverage lies in commercial wealth, good relations with Somocista officials and their links to Saudi patrons.

11.name: Los Centinelas del Califato
11.text:
The Sentinels of the Caliphate are a tiny secret circle of young Muslims of Palestinian descent who encountered Hizb ut-Tahrir pamphlets while studying in Amman. They read Taqiuddin al-Nabhani's call to restore the caliphate and pass his writings among a few trusted friends.

The circle rejects nationalism, democracy and both superpowers and calls for a single Islamic state for all Muslims. It has no base in Nicaragua, but its members are disciplined, secretive and convinced of their cause.

12.name: La Hermandad de Masaya
12.text:
The Masaya Brotherhood is a small study circle of educated Muslims of Arab descent in Masaya and Managua who read Hassan al-Banna and Sayyid Qutb and follow the fortunes of the Muslim Brotherhood in Egypt and Jordan. Its members are merchants, doctors and students.

The circle promotes piety, mutual aid and an Islamic social order built through education and charity, and it keeps its distance from both superpowers and from the dictatorship. Its influence is minimal, limited to welfare and religious instruction within the small Muslim minority.

13.name: La Dinastía
13.text:
The Dynasty is the Somoza family as a power bloc in its own right: an economic empire of estates, cattle ranches, the national airline, shipping, construction and state concessions, managed by family members and trusted retainers around President Anastasio Somoza Debayle. It treats Nicaragua almost as family property.

The bloc's only ideology is the survival and enrichment of the family, pursued through monopolies, state contracts and control of the Guard. It is pragmatic rather than doctrinaire. Its leverage is enormous: the family's wealth and patronage bind officers, officials and businessmen to its fate.

14.name: Partido Conservador Tradicionalista
14.text:
The Traditionalist Conservative Party is the main body of Nicaragua's historic Conservative Party and the principal legal opposition to the Somozas. Its leader, the ophthalmologist Fernando Agüero Rocha, headed the opposition ticket in 1967 and the protest that ended in the massacre of 22 January in Managua.

The Conservatives defend Catholic tradition, the old landed families of Granada, private property and constitutional government, and they demand free elections and an end to dynastic rule. Their leverage lies in a loyal following among historic Conservative families, the Church and regions hostile to the Liberals.

15.name: Banco de América
15.text:
The Banco de America group is one of the two great private financial groups of Nicaragua, built in the 1950s around the Pellas family's sugar and rum interests and the old Conservative families of Granada. Together with its rival BANIC, it controls much of the credit, agro-export and industrial investment outside the Somoza empire.

The group favours free enterprise, export growth and stability, and it resents the Somozas' growing encroachment on private business while fearing revolution even more. Its leverage lies in capital, credit and links to Conservative politics.

16.name: Instituto Nicaragüense de Desarrollo
16.text:
The Nicaraguan Development Institute was founded in 1963 by private businessmen who wanted the private sector, not the Somoza state, to lead the country's modernisation. It promotes management training, cooperatives and business-led social programmes.

INDE champions free enterprise, competition, open markets and responsible capitalism as the answer to poverty and communism, and it quietly criticises the corruption and favouritism of the Somoza economy. It is close to American business circles. Its leverage lies in its members' investments and their standing as modern, independent entrepreneurs.

17.name: Defensores del Xolotlán
17.text:
The Defenders of the Xolotlán are a loose group of university scientists, physicians, fishermen and journalists alarmed by the pollution of Lake Managua, known by its indigenous name Xolotlán. Untreated sewage from the capital and waste from a new chemical plant on the shore are poisoning its waters.

They demand sewage treatment, controls on industrial waste and protection of the lakes and forests of the Pacific region, staying clear of bloc politics. Their leverage is small, resting on scientific reports, press coverage in La Prensa and the health concerns of Managua's residents.

18.name: Comunidad de Solentiname
18.text:
The Solentiname Community was founded in 1966 by the priest and poet Ernesto Cardenal on an archipelago in Lake Nicaragua. Its peasant families read the Gospel together, paint, write poetry and run cooperatives, and the community has become a beacon for radical Christians across Latin America.

Inspired by liberation theology and the Cuban Revolution, it calls for social justice, communal ownership and the liberation of the poor from the dictatorship and capitalism, independent of both blocs. Its leverage lies in moral prestige, international cultural fame and its influence on young Christians drifting toward revolution.

19.name: Partido Comunista de Nicaragua
19.text:
The Communist Party of Nicaragua broke away from the Nicaraguan Socialist Party in the late 1960s, accusing its leadership of passivity and opportunism. It is a small underground organisation rooted among workers and union militants who want a more combative communist line.

The party rejects both the PSN's caution and the foquismo of the Sandinistas, insisting on a workers' revolution built through strikes and independent mass organisation, and it guards its independence from Moscow's directives. Its leverage lies in a few militant unions and dedicated cadres.

20.name: Las Turbas Nicolasianas
20.text:
Nicolasa's Mobs are the Somocista street crowds led by Nicolasa Sevilla, a fiercely loyal party activist who has organised gangs of urban poor to defend the Somozas since the 1940s. They are mobilised to break up opposition rallies, attack newspapers and fill the streets on the dynasty's behalf.

The mobs combine populist appeals to the poor with personal devotion to the Somoza family and hatred for Conservatives, students and 'communists'. Their leverage lies in numbers, intimidation and the protection of the National Guard.

21.name: Los Camisas Azules
21.text:
The Blue Shirts are the surviving veterans and admirers of the 1930s Nicaraguan blue-shirted movement, an authoritarian Catholic youth militia inspired by Spanish Falangism and Italian Fascism. Their heirs persist among Hispanist intellectuals, conservative Catholic circles and hardline anti-communists.

They dream of a corporatist, Catholic and Hispanic state, purged of liberalism and communism and led by a disciplined national vanguard. They admire Franco's Spain. Their numbers are small, but their ideas resonate with officers and Somocistas who want harsher measures against the left.

22.name: Guardia Nacional de Nicaragua
22.text:
The National Guard of Nicaragua was created in 1927 under US Marine supervision as a combined army and police force, and since 1936 it has been the private instrument of the Somoza family. President Anastasio Somoza Debayle, a West Point graduate, is also its Jefe Director.

The Guard is fiercely anti-communist, trained and equipped by the United States, and loyal to the family rather than the nation. It enforces order, collects bribes and runs smuggling and prostitution rackets. Its leverage is total: it monopolises force, controls customs and communications, and keeps the dynasty in power.

23.name: House of Clarence
23.text:
The House of Clarence is the royal line of the Mosquito Kingdom, which ruled the Caribbean coast under British protection until Nicaragua incorporated the reserve in 1894. Its descendants and the memory of the Miskito kings live on among Miskito and Creole communities of the Atlantic coast, sustained by the Moravian Church.

The monarchists seek autonomy, communal land rights, protection of the Miskito and English languages and respect for coastal traditions, and they distrust the Spanish-speaking governments of Managua. Their leverage lies in the deep loyalty of coastal communities that the state barely controls.
